content.text:
Your best first contribution is [Entire CLI issue #2001: preserve OpenCode prompts when events arrive in sequence](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2001).

It is unassigned, has no competing discussion, is tightly scoped, and directly matches the lifecycle/event-ordering work you have already done in [LegionCode](https://github.com/Puneet-Pal-Singh/LegionCode)—especially your [turn-scoped interruption work](https://github.com/Puneet-Pal-Singh/LegionCode/commit/60a7aa5a).

## Why #2001 is the right first move

Entire’s generated OpenCode plugin receives:

1. `message.updated`, containing message metadata but no prompt text.
2. `message.part.updated`, containing the actual prompt.

Today one `seenUserMessages` set represents two different facts:

- “The turn was activated.”
- “The prompt was captured.”

The first event marks the message seen and starts an empty-prompt turn. The second event is then ignored.

That is a small bug, but the reasoning behind the fix is valuable: lifecycle activation and content availability are different states. That maps directly to LegionCode’s explicit separation of thread, turn, run attempt, transcript part, and terminal lifecycle state.

The ideal contribution shape is:

- Add a regression covering the exact event order.
- Preserve early activation so commits still see an active session.
- Preserve the later prompt without creating a duplicate logical turn.
- Replace the overloaded boolean/set semantics with explicit state.
- Avoid introducing a second prompt/transcript authority.

This should be a narrow PR around:

- `cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/entire_plugin.ts`
- `cmd/entire/cli/agent/opencode/hooks_test.go`
- Possibly one focused integration test if the existing string-based installation tests cannot prove runtime behavior.

### Comment to post before coding

Entire explicitly requires discussion before implementation. I would post:

> Hi, I’d like to work on this. I traced the current path on main and think the underlying problem is that `seenUserMessages` conflates two states: the turn has been activated, and the prompt content has been captured.
>
> I’d start with a regression for `message.updated → message.part.updated`, proving that the session becomes active early, the real prompt survives, and exactly one logical turn is created.
>
> Before implementing, I’d like to confirm the intended enrichment contract: should a later text part update the already-active turn through an idempotent `turn-start`, or should the plugin retain separate “turn started” and “prompt captured” state and use another existing hook path? I want to preserve early commit safety without adding a parallel prompt store.
>
> If that direction matches the intended lifecycle semantics, I’d be happy to take it.

That comment demonstrates substantially more judgment than “can you assign this to me?”

## Best follow-up: #1730

After landing a smaller PR, tackle [#1730: merge-aware shadow checkpoint reachability](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1730).

This is the deepest LegionCode overlap. It concerns:

- Durable session identity.
- Worktree identity.
- Branch-origin metadata.
- False positives across merged histories.
- False negatives from first-parent traversal.
- Keeping temporary checkpoint projections from leaking across branches.

The issue originally says Entire lacks origin-branch metadata. Current main now has a `State.Branch` field and writes branch metadata into checkpoints, but it is not automatically sufficient:

- It records the branch at turn start, not necessarily immutable session origin.
- A branch can be created or switched during a turn.
- Branch names can be renamed.
- Older checkpoints have no value.
- Filtering currently happens at the shadow-branch level before checkpoint metadata is read.

That makes this an excellent architecture contribution, but not a safe first PR. Start with a design comment that distinguishes:

- Immutable session origin.
- Current branch.
- Checkpoint-write branch.
- Worktree identity.
- Legacy fallback behavior.

This is almost exactly the kind of canonical identity work formalized in LegionCode’s [`platform-protocol`](https://github.com/Puneet-Pal-Singh/LegionCode/tree/main/packages/platform-protocol) and [`git-service`](https://github.com/Puneet-Pal-Singh/LegionCode/tree/main/packages/git-service).

|---|---:|---|
| [#2115: per-hook timeout budgets](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2115) | Very high | First contribute measurements from running Entire on LegionCode; implementation needs maintainer decisions. |

| [skills #29: untrusted session handoff](https://github.com/entireio/skills/issues/29) | High security fit | Good issue, but the reporter already offered to implement it. Don’t snipe it. |
| [git-sync #67: redirect semantics](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/issues/67) | Medium-high | Solid Go/security contribution, but less directly connected to LegionCode’s agent lifecycle story. |
| [#2033: generic checkpoint remote](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2033) | High strategic fit | Too broad for a first PR; depends on checkpoint-store/provider architecture. |

## Issues I would avoid taking now

Several apparently available issues already have someone doing the work:

- [#1836](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1836): contributor and maintainer are already deep in performance design.
- [#2089](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2089): another contributor has proposed the implementation.
- [#1924](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1924): already has draft PR [#1948](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1948).
- [external-agents #67](https://github.com/entireio/external-agents/issues/67): all adapter fixes now have open PRs.
- [external-agents #61](https://github.com/entireio/external-agents/issues/61): covered by PR [#62](https://github.com/entireio/external-agents/pull/62).
- [#2008](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2008): excellent concurrency bug, but the reporter explicitly offered to implement it.

## How Entire and LegionCode connect

Entire is not primarily another coding agent. It is a Git-native provenance and context layer around agents. LegionCode is an agent workspace/runtime. Their boundaries are complementary:

- LegionCode creates typed turn, tool, approval, artifact, and terminal lifecycle records.
- Entire associates agent sessions and transcripts with Git checkpoints.
- LegionCode’s harness adapter boundary resembles Entire’s built-in/external agent adapters.
- LegionCode’s canonical completed-turn artifacts align with Entire’s checkpoint and explain model.
- LegionCode’s worktree isolation and Git authority align with Entire’s checkpoint-ref concurrency problems.
- Entire Graph could eventually become a repository-context provider for LegionCode’s context engine.
- A future LegionCode external-agent adapter could expose LegionCode sessions to Entire—but Entire’s own guide explicitly says a new agent adapter is not a first-PR project.

The strongest longer-term story is:

```text
LegionCode turn/run lifecycle
→ Entire-compatible session adapter
→ Entire checkpoint attached to LegionCode artifact/commit/PR
→ Entire search/graph context available to later LegionCode turns
```

Do not pitch or build that first. Earn trust through one narrow correctness contribution, then propose it with evidence.

## Recommended sequence

1. Comment on [#2001](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2001) and wait for approval.
2. Install Entire and use it while making the contribution; their [contribution guide](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) strongly values `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers.
3. Submit one narrow PR with event-order regression coverage.
4. Address every automated review comment—Entire explicitly blocks maintainer review on unresolved Copilot feedback.
5. Dogfood Entire on LegionCode and collect hook latency/checkpoint behavior.
6. Use that evidence on [#2115](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2115) or write the identity analysis for [#1730](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1730).
7. Only after those contributions, discuss a LegionCode adapter or Graph/context integration.

I worked on Entire #2001 and treated the bug as a lifecycle-state problem: early turn activation and later prompt availability were being collapsed into one flag. I added event-order regression coverage and kept one logical turn authority. I also dogfooded the change through LegionCode. I’d value any feedback on whether this demonstrates the kind of engineering judgment you were looking for.

That makes the referral conversation about demonstrated thinking, not about asking again.

content.text:
Yes—moving this task into the cloned Entire CLI project was the right decision. It let me inspect the exact implementation, documentation, Git history, and repository instructions without guessing.

## Best contribution: scale checkpoint discovery by the requested history

The strongest genuinely new gap I found is:

> `entire checkpoint list` and branch-scoped `entire checkpoint explain` enumerate every checkpoint ref on the remote before examining which checkpoint IDs the current branch actually references.

The current sequence is visible in [explain.go](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:2500):

1. Run remote discovery using `git ls-remote refs/entire/checkpoints/*`.
2. Build a map containing every checkpoint.
3. Walk the branch history.
4. Keep only checkpoints whose IDs appear in commit trailers.
5. Finally truncate to the requested `--limit`.

The storage implementation confirms that remote discovery lists the complete namespace in [refs_store.go](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go:500), and the architecture document explicitly says it may query and merge complete listings from multiple remotes in [ref-checkpoint-backend.md](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/docs/architecture/ref-checkpoint-backend.md:121).

I measured the public `entireio/cli-checkpoints` remote today:

- 1,122 checkpoint refs
- approximately 0.85 seconds just to enumerate them
- this cost is paid even if the user requests only 10 checkpoints
- the work grows with the repository’s lifetime, not with `--limit`

That is still manageable today, which likely explains why nobody has reported it. But it is structurally unbounded.

The especially interesting part: the original per-checkpoint-ref proposal said branch-scoped flows should inspect code history to find relevant checkpoint IDs and then resolve those IDs directly. The current implementation does the reverse. See [issue #1471](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1471).

### Why the competitor research exposed this

[Code.Storage](https://code.storage/) is explicitly optimized for machine workloads, advertising 30+ concurrent writes, observed Git traffic above 500 requests per second per repository, and machine-oriented APIs.

Cursor’s [Git at any scale](https://cursor.com/blog/git-at-any-scale) describes an architecture designed for massive monorepos and millions of small agent-created repositories. Its important lesson for Entire is not to reproduce Cursor’s storage backend; it is to ensure every operation is proportional to the working set being requested.

Origin also tightly connects repositories to agents and automations, meaning repository metadata volume will increasingly be machine-generated rather than human-bounded. [Origin integrations](https://cursor.com/docs/origin/integrations) supports cloud agents and source-control-triggered automations directly.

Entire’s checkpoint model is excellent for this future, but globally enumerating an ever-growing ref namespace for a branch-local query is the wrong scaling shape.

### Proposed issue

**Title**

> Avoid full remote checkpoint-ref enumeration for branch-scoped list and explain

**Core proposal**

- Walk the bounded branch history first.
- Collect checkpoint IDs and commit timestamps from `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers.
- Sort and apply the display limit.
- Resolve only those checkpoint IDs through the existing checkpoint reader.
- Let the existing exact-ref fetcher retrieve a missing checkpoint from another machine.
- Preserve global enumeration only for operations that genuinely need repository-wide discovery, such as commit-less imports.
- Preserve git-branch/git-refs routing and multi-remote fallback behavior.

This changes the remote work approximately from:

```text
O(all checkpoint refs in repository)
```

to:

```text
O(checkpoints in bounded branch history)
```

The implementation can probably remain entirely inside the CLI read path. It does not require a server feature or checkpoint format change.

### Good first implementation slice

A maintainer-friendly first PR could contain:

- A regression test proving branch-scoped listing can find a remote-only checkpoint through its known trailer without invoking the global remote-ref lister.
- Exact-ref hydration only after sorting and truncation.
- Existing second-device behavior preserved.
- A synthetic benchmark or test with a very large fake remote namespace demonstrating that work depends on the branch limit, not total ref count.
- Documentation updated to distinguish global storage enumeration from branch-scoped resolution.

I searched open and closed issues and PRs using the exact implementation names and related phrases. [PR #1771](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1771) and [PR #1956](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1956) introduced the current enumeration behavior, but I found no issue or PR addressing its scaling shape.

### Draft maintainer message

> While studying the refs-v1 discovery path, I noticed that branch-scoped `checkpoint list`/`explain` first enumerate every remote `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` ref, then walk commit trailers and discard everything unrelated to the branch. The original per-ref design in #1471 suggested the opposite order: discover checkpoint IDs from branch history, then resolve those IDs directly.
>
> The public CLI checkpoint remote currently has 1,122 refs and enumeration takes roughly 0.85s for me. The cost is independent of `--limit` and grows for the lifetime of the repository.
>
> Would you be open to changing only the branch-scoped path to:
>
> 1. scan bounded commit history,
> 2. collect and truncate trailer checkpoint IDs,
> 3. resolve/fetch only those refs,
>
> while retaining full enumeration for genuinely repository-wide or commit-less discovery?
>
> I would start with regression tests around second-device discovery and multi-remote fallback before changing the implementation.

That message demonstrates architectural thinking without overselling the problem.

## Second idea: detect concurrent-session file overlap

Entire intentionally allows multiple conversations in the same worktree. At session start, it currently gives only a count and says their work may be included together, as shown in [lifecycle.go](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/lifecycle.go:176).

Cursor takes the stronger isolation approach: [each concurrent task gets its own worktree](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees).

I would not propose forcing worktree locks in Entire—that contradicts current behavior. A better new idea is:

> When active sessions in the same worktree have overlapping `FilesTouched`, show the overlap in `entire status` and the session-start warning.

For example:

```text
2 active conversations overlap on:
  cmd/entire/cli/explain.go
  cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go
```

This would turn a generic concurrency warning into actionable information without blocking anybody.

This connects strongly to your LegionCode experience with:

- scoped execution leases,
- worktree/run-attempt isolation,
- immutable Git snapshots,
- concurrent mutation fencing.

I found no public Entire issue specifically proposing active-session file-overlap detection. This is a good secondary discussion, but the scaling issue is cleaner because it has a precise, testable performance invariant.

## Third idea: durable run segments across local/cloud handoff

Cursor now supports moving an agent session between local and cloud environments, and Origin integrates local agents, cloud agents, and automations. See [Cursor 3](https://cursor.com/blog/cursor-3) and [Origin integrations](https://cursor.com/docs/origin/integrations).

Entire’s persisted checkpoint metadata currently records agent, model, session, turn, branch, files, metrics, and attribution, but not a structured execution segment or handoff lineage; see [metadata.go](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/api/checkpoint/metadata.go:388).

A future contract might distinguish:

```text
logical_run_id
segment_id
parent_segment_id
execution_environment: local | cloud | automation
handoff_reason
```

That would let Entire answer:

- Is this one durable run continued on another machine?
- Was a checkpoint produced locally, by a cloud agent, or by automation?
- Which segment preceded a handoff?
- Did two environments concurrently continue the same logical run?

I found no exact public issue for this. However, it changes checkpoint schema and requires agent-provided identity, so it should remain a design discussion until maintainers confirm the direction.

## Ideas we should not claim as new

The duplicate search eliminated several tempting directions:

- Pre-flight/context manifests: already [issue #763](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/763).
- Multi-repository sessions: [#529](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/529), [#1439](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1439), and active [PR #1959](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1959).
- Push-queue concurrency: [#2008](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2008).
- Merge-aware ephemeral reachability: [#1730](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1730).
- Remote checkpoint availability audit: previously attempted in [PR #1881](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1881).
- Mandatory worktree isolation: inconsistent with Entire’s intentionally supported multi-session behavior.

## My recommendation

Lead with the branch-scoped checkpoint discovery scaling issue. It is:

- new relative to the public issue/PR history I checked;
- grounded in current code rather than speculation;
- directly inspired by the competitor research;
- measurable today;
- bounded enough for a strong external contribution;
- an excellent demonstration of how you think about agent-scale infrastructure.

Do not implement it yet. Entire’s [contribution rules](/Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/CONTRIBUTING.md:9) require opening an issue and waiting for maintainer approval first. The next move should be refining the issue body and posting it for discussion.

I think the previous issues which open by people might be stale we should open our Own Issues and work on it,
There would be multiple things this projects needs they recently added support for sub-agents.
We can look for existing issues also. If they align with the gap we found in code.
We can add some agentic functionality, improve something. Fix someghing, cut latency, there are many things I can contribute to.
Help me find it and lets discuss , so we will work on them proactively.

Agreed on being proactive, but I’d separate “stale issue” from “unclaimed problem”: we should verify current `main`, reproduce or measure each gap, then open a fresh issue only when it adds materially new evidence or scope. I’ll rescan recent sub-agent work, latency paths, and open PR/issue activity, then give you a short contribution portfolio—not a random list.

Important discovery: your fork’s `main` is 807 commits behind `upstream/main`. I based this analysis on the freshly fetched upstream commit `077859742`, not the stale local checkout.

## Best contribution to propose ourselves

I recommend opening a narrowly scoped issue:

**“Preserve the model used by each subagent in durable task records”**

This is a real, currently unreported gap:

- Cursor already sends `subagent_model`.
- Codex subagent hooks already populate the normalized `Event.Model`.
- Cursor’s parser reads `subagent_model` but drops it when constructing the lifecycle event.
- `TaskRecord`, `TaskPayload`, and the committed `tasks/<tool-use-id>/task.json` schema have no model field.

You can see the discontinuity directly:

- [Cursor parses rich subagent metadata](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/types.go#L145-L189)
- [Cursor drops the model when creating the event](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/agent/cursor/lifecycle.go#L185-L229)
- [The durable task record has no model](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go#L465-L512)
- [The committed `task.json` also omits it](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go#L1297-L1315)

Why this is valuable: Entire can currently show what a child did, its files, transcript, timings, and sometimes tokens—but not which model actually performed the delegated task. The parent and child can use different models. That prevents meaningful analysis of delegation quality, cost, and model selection.

Suggested first-issue scope:

- Add optional `Model` to `session.TaskRecord`.
- Carry it through `checkpoint.TaskPayload`.
- Persist it as optional `model` in `task.json`.
- Populate it for Codex and Cursor.
- Preserve launch-time model through completion/reconciliation.
- Add backward-compatibility and materialization tests.
- Omit blank models.

Keep these explicitly out of the first PR:

- UI changes.
- Status/outcome normalization.
- Cursor’s free-text `summary`.
- Parent/child graph redesign.
- Message/tool/loop counts.
- API changes outside the CLI repository.

That restraint is important. It gives maintainers a small, useful schema extension instead of asking them to approve an entire observability system.

A good draft issue opening would be:

> Current durable subagent task records preserve type, description, transcript, files, tokens, and timing, but not the model that executed the task. This information is already available for Codex through `Event.Model`, and Cursor exposes a dedicated `subagent_model`, which is parsed but discarded. As a result, committed task records cannot distinguish a parent and child using different models or support later delegation cost/quality analysis.

We should wait for maintainer approval before implementing, as required by the repository workflow.

## Best performance contribution

Do not open a duplicate issue here. Claim a focused slice of [#2091: Hook latency remaining work](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2091).

The strongest unclaimed slice is **item 2b: compact transcript generation happens twice during Stop**. A maintainer explicitly described it as the smaller, self-contained option and invited a contributor to claim it.

Current code confirms it still exists:

- Initial checkpoint writing calls `writeCompactTranscript`.
- Stop finalization calls it again.
- Each call uses `FullWithBoundary`.
- `FullWithBoundary` itself runs both full and delta compaction to calculate the boundary.

So one Stop can traverse/compact the cumulative transcript as many as four times. The issue measured roughly **904 ms out of a 2.5-second Stop** before other recent changes.

# Concurrent-session file overlap

This is a valid new feature, but we need to describe precisely what it detects.

Entire already tracks `SessionState.FilesTouched`. It uses this for:

- attributing committed files to sessions;
- carry-forward after partial commits;
- deciding whether ended sessions still contain work;
- merging subagent files into the parent session;
- checking whether staged files overlap a session during commit processing.

What Entire does not currently do is compare the pending file claims of two live sessions and surface that relationship to the user.

That is the gap.

## Important limitation in the screenshot proposal

The screenshot suggests displaying exact overlap in the session-start warning. A newly created session has not touched any files yet, so no overlap exists to report at session start.

The current session-start warning can only say:

> Other conversations already exist in this workspace.

Actual overlap becomes knowable only after both sessions have recorded file activity.

Depending on the agent, that happens:

- immediately after individual tool calls;
- at subagent completion;
- or only at turn end, after transcript/file extraction.

Therefore, the first version should surface overlap in `entire status`, not promise exact session-start detection.

## Recommended definition

Call it an **attribution overlap**, not necessarily a filesystem conflict:

> Two non-ended sessions in the same physical worktree both have the same normalized repository-relative path in their pending `FilesTouched`.

This distinction matters. `FilesTouched` means both sessions claim work involving the path. It does not prove they wrote simultaneously or that Git contains conflicting hunks.

### Include

- ACTIVE sessions.
- IDLE but non-ended sessions.
- Sessions whose owner exited but still have pending files.
- Subagent work merged into a parent’s `FilesTouched`.
- Modified, created, and deleted paths.
- Exact normalized path matches.

### Exclude

- Sessions in different worktrees.
- Ended sessions.
- Empty or unknown worktree paths.
- Directory-prefix matches such as `src/` versus `src/a.go`.
- Semantic conflicts between different files.
- Case-folded matching in the initial implementation.
- Automatic locking or blocking.

Different worktrees must remain isolated even when they modify the same relative path. That makes LegionCode an excellent negative dogfood case: two isolated LegionCode runs editing `apps/web/foo.ts` should produce no warning because their physical worktrees differ.

Cursor uses the same isolation principle: its worktree feature gives separate tasks separate checkouts specifically to avoid conflicts. It is available through the Agents Window, IDE worktree skills, and Cursor CLI—not only cloud agents. [Cursor worktree documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees).

## A substantial first slice

A good first implementation is larger than merely printing one warning but remains reviewable.

### 1. Shared overlap computation

Introduce a pure function operating on session state:

```go
type SessionFileOverlap struct {
    WorktreePath string
    File         string
    SessionIDs   []string
}
```

The computation should:

- filter through the canonical `State.IsEnded()` predicate;
- canonicalize worktree paths consistently;
- deduplicate duplicate paths within one session;
- group by physical worktree;
- identify paths claimed by at least two sessions;
- sort worktrees, files, and session IDs deterministically;
- avoid filesystem or Git operations.

Complexity should be approximately:

```text
O(total FilesTouched entries + sorting)
```

Do not implement it as all-session-pairs × all-file-pairs.

### 2. Human `entire status`

Render the warning once per worktree group, not repeatedly under every session:

```text
! 2 sessions overlap on 2 pending files:
  cmd/entire/cli/explain.go
    codex · 01ABC…
    cursor · 01XYZ…

  cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/refs_store.go
    codex · 01ABC…
    cursor · 01XYZ…
```

For a large collision set, cap the displayed paths and print:

```text
… and 14 more; run `entire status --json` for the complete list
```

This prevents an accidental hundred-file status dump.

### 3. Machine-readable status

Add a top-level collection rather than duplicating overlap lists into every session:

```json
{
  "session_file_overlaps": [
    {
      "worktree_path": "/repo",
      "file": "cmd/entire/cli/explain.go",
      "session_ids": ["session-a", "session-b"]
    }
  ]
}
```

This would let LegionCode or another orchestrator consume the warning without parsing terminal output.

### 4. Tests

The first PR should include:

- two live sessions, same worktree, same path → overlap;
- three sessions on one path → one entry containing three IDs;
- same path in different worktrees → no overlap;
- ended session → excluded;
- IDLE session with pending files → included;
- exited session with pending files → included;
- duplicate paths in one session → no false multi-session overlap;
- paths sorted deterministically;
- human output capped while JSON remains complete;
- unknown worktree path → excluded;
- empty `FilesTouched` → excluded.

This is significant enough to demonstrate architecture, algorithm choice, UX design, JSON-contract thinking, and testing discipline.

## What should be a later slice

Immediate warnings after a tool edits a colliding file are attractive but should not be in the first PR.

They require answering harder questions:

- Can every agent display output from `PostToolUse` hooks?
- Should a warning be sent to the user, the model, or both?
- How do we avoid repeating the warning on every edit?
- Where is the “already warned for this overlap fingerprint” state stored?
- How does it behave for agents that discover files only at turn end?
- Could reading all session files make a latency-sensitive tool hook too slow?

After the status foundation exists, we could add a one-shot warning for agents with reliable per-tool hooks.

Enabling Entire in [LegionCode](https://github.com/Puneet-Pal-Singh/LegionCode) is useful, but normal LegionCode execution will mostly test the negative case because it isolates runs in separate workspaces/worktrees.

Use two scenarios:

2. **Positive reproduction:** two agent sessions run directly in the same disposable checkout and edit the same test file without committing. Expected: `entire status` reports the overlap.

The automated test should construct isolated session states directly; it should not require real paid agent E2E calls.

Yes—you’re getting it right. Your objection shows that the proposed “session file overlap in `entire status`” feature is weakly motivated. I would drop it as our primary contribution.

The confusion came from mixing three different kinds of overlap:

| Concept | What it means | Correct place |
|---|---|---|
| Shared-worktree collision | Two live conversations mutate the same physical checkout | Prevent with worktree isolation |
| Git merge conflict | Two branches make incompatible textual changes | Merge/rebase/PR |
| Implementation overlap | Two branches independently implement similar functionality | Review/compare workflow |

### Is an Entire session a chat?

Approximately, yes.

An Entire session corresponds to an agent’s conversation/session identity. For Cursor, Entire directly maps Cursor’s `conversation_id` to its session ID. One session can contain:

- Multiple user prompts and agent turns
- Many file changes
- Subagent tasks attributed back to the parent session
- Possibly several checkpoints

But these are not equivalent:

```text
session ≠ worktree ≠ branch ≠ commit ≠ pull request
```

Several sessions can run in one worktree, and one session can produce multiple checkpoints or commits.

### Why would both sessions need recorded file activity?

Only to calculate this set:

```text
session_A.FilesTouched ∩ session_B.FilesTouched
```

Before both sessions have touched files, there is nothing to intersect.

But this tells us only:

> Both conversations claimed activity involving the same path.

It does not prove:

- They edited simultaneously
- One overwrote the other
- Their changes conflict
- They implemented the same feature
- Their eventual PRs will conflict
- One duplicated the other’s work

Even two sessions touching the same file may edit different functions and merge cleanly. Conversely, changes in different files may conflict semantically.

So your instinct is correct: `FilesTouched` intersection is not a meaningful implementation-overlap detector.

### The 70-session problem

Also correct.

If 70 sessions legitimately touched `apps/web/foo.ts`, listing 70 session IDs would create noise rather than insight. Filtering to currently active sessions reduces the scale, but doesn’t fix the conceptual problem.

Immediate warnings would be especially bad:

> “Another conversation has edited this file.”

Independent sessions should not constantly receive information about other sessions. It would pollute model context, distract users, add hook latency, and undermine independent experimentation.

I retract the “later one-shot warning” suggestion. We should not propose that.

### Does this matter when merging two session PRs?

That is where overlap can matter—but it should be computed from branches or diffs, not session metadata.

Suppose:

```text
PR A: base → branch-a
PR B: base → branch-b
```

A useful review system might compare:

- Files changed by both PRs
- Overlapping diff hunks
- Symbols/functions modified by both
- Duplicate tests or implementations
- Dependency/API interactions
- Whether the two branches merge cleanly
- Whether one PR supersedes the other

That could become a genuine multi-agent review capability for Entire, but it is a different and substantially larger product idea. It would probably belong around `entire review`, checkpoints, or branch comparison—not ordinary `entire status`.

### What Cursor does

Cursor’s main answer is isolation, not overlap warnings.

Cursor says each task can get an isolated checkout, and recommends worktrees specifically for running several agents without conflicts. `/best-of-n` runs the same request in separate worktrees and lets the user compare candidates; it explicitly does not merge them automatically. Cursor subagents share the parent checkout by default, but users can request isolated worktrees when concurrent editing is needed. [Cursor worktree documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees), [Cursor subagent documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/subagents)

That aligns with your view:

```text
independent execution → separate worktrees
comparison → after results exist
integration → deliberate merge/apply/review
```

Cursor Origin is lower-level Git infrastructure. Its concurrency mechanisms concern pushes, reference transactions, replication, consistency, and scaling—not warnings that two agent chats touched the same file. [Cursor’s Git at any scale](https://cursor.com/blog/git-at-any-scale)

### What Code.Storage does

Code.Storage is also infrastructure rather than an agent-session coordinator. Its public material advertises concurrent writes, consistent replicas, Git hosting, SDK access, and high-scale machine-generated repositories. I found no public feature for detecting file overlap among agent conversations. [Code.Storage](https://code.storage/)

“30+ concurrent writes” there means storage-level Git operations—not 30 agents sharing one working directory and being warned about common files.

### Is the LegionCode worktree design good?

Yes. LegionCode giving each run its own physical worktree is the right architecture.

Two LegionCode runs can both modify:

```text
apps/web/foo.ts
```

without interfering because the paths exist in separate checkouts. Afterward you can:

- Select one result
- Compare both implementations
- Merge one into the other
- Open separate PRs
- Detect real Git conflicts

Enabling Entire inside each worktree could add durable conversation/checkpoint provenance to each run. That is a credible LegionCode–Entire integration direction.

But it does not make session-overlap warnings valuable. It mostly demonstrates that isolation eliminates the underlying shared-filesystem problem.

### Recommendation

Drop “surface pending file overlap in `entire status`.”

The stronger direction hidden inside your question is:

> Compare the outputs of multiple isolated agent sessions or checkpoints during review.

That is actually agentic, connects naturally to LegionCode, and resembles Cursor’s best-of-N workflow while giving Entire a possible differentiation: comparing not only final diffs, but also the checkpoint history, reasoning provenance, tests, and implementation decisions behind them.

We should investigate Entire’s existing `review`, checkpoint comparison, and subagent task records before deciding whether that becomes a new issue.

Let’s put all three ideas in the arena and let them fight.

## 1. Scale checkpoint discovery by requested history

### Five points supporting it

1. **There is a concrete scaling mismatch.** A branch view requesting roughly 100 checkpoints can enumerate every checkpoint ref in the repository first.

2. **PRs #1771 and #1956 do not eliminate it.** They improve remote discovery and lazy hydration, but remote ref enumeration is still repository-wide.

3. **The invariant is measurable.** Work should scale primarily with requested branch history, not total checkpoint count.

4. **It fits Entire’s direction.** More agents and checkpoints will increase the ref count dramatically, especially in monorepos.

5. **It can become a bounded engineering contribution.** Optimize branch-scoped listing while leaving inherently global commands unchanged.

### Five points roasting it

1. **We have not demonstrated actual pain.** “This is theoretically O(N)” is weaker than “10,000 refs make this command take eight seconds.”

2. **Git servers may still scan their ref namespace.** Sending exact patterns reduces response payload but does not guarantee proportional server work.

3. **History-first discovery has edge cases.** Imported checkpoints, older formats, missing trailers, remote-only history, and partially fetched repositories complicate it.

4. **The apparent redundant work may be deliberate.** The current store abstraction provides one consistent discovery path; bypassing it could fragment semantics.

5. **Maintainers may prefer caching or server-side indexing.** We could produce an elegant local optimization that becomes irrelevant to their intended architecture.

**Verdict:** Best original idea so far, but only after producing a benchmark/reproduction. **7.5/10.**

---

## 2. Detect concurrent-session file overlap

### Five points supporting it

1. Entire already warns about multiple active conversations in one workspace, but the warning is generic.

2. `FilesTouched` and `WorktreePath` already exist, making a status-only implementation comparatively inexpensive.

3. It could occasionally explain ambiguous attribution when multiple conversations share one physical checkout.

4. The calculation can be deterministic and linear over recorded paths.

5. It initially appeared connected to multi-agent concurrency, which is strategically relevant.

### Five points roasting it

1. **It detects path intersection, not conflict.** Same file does not mean incompatible edits or duplicate implementation.

2. **It observes the problem too late.** Once two agents edit the same physical checkout, changes are already mixed.

3. **Worktree isolation is the correct solution.** Cursor and LegionCode prevent interference structurally.

4. **It would produce terrible noise.** Popular files touched by many sessions could generate large, unactionable lists.

5. **It creates false confidence.** Different files can conflict semantically, while the same file can merge perfectly.

**Verdict:** Technically implementable, product-wise confused. Correctly dropped. **2/10.**

---

## 3. Durable run segments across local/cloud handoff

### Five points supporting it

1. **The industry is moving toward portable execution.** Agent work can move among local machines, cloud environments, automations, and subagents.

2. **It aligns strongly with Entire’s core value.** Entire is about durable agent history and provenance, not merely final Git diffs.

3. **A logical run may outlive one agent-native session.** Segment lineage could preserve continuity while recording where each part executed.

4. **It could improve auditability.** Teams could determine which environment produced a checkpoint and how execution reached it.

5. **It connects naturally to LegionCode.** A durable run spanning orchestrated workspaces, retries, and handoffs is close to LegionCode’s domain.

### Five points roasting it

1. **We invented a schema before proving a user problem.** `logical_run_id`, `segment_id`, and `handoff_reason` look architectural, but what command needs them today?

2. **Entire may not observe the handoff.** Cursor or another agent must provide a reliable parent identity. Entire cannot infer lineage safely from files or branches.

3. **“Handoff” means different things across providers.** Resume, fork, cloud delegation, retry, subagent creation, and migration are not necessarily one abstraction.

4. **It changes a durable compatibility contract.** Checkpoint schemas, readers, old clients, imported checkpoints, and server APIs may all be affected.

5. **Entire already has adjacent primitives.** Session continuation, `PreviousSessionID`, adopt/resume, task records, and checkpoint lineage must be studied before adding another identity graph.

**Verdict:** Strong strategic concept, weak first contribution. This is a design discussion requiring a real end-to-end handoff example—not a speculative schema PR. **4.5/10 today, potentially 9/10 later.**

## Final ranking

1. **Checkpoint discovery scaling** — pursue after benchmark proof.
2. **Durable run segments** — continue researching, but do not implement yet.
3. **Concurrent file overlap** — leave buried.

## The “bro, you need a job” point

Bro, don’t spend the entire war sharpening the axe.

A clean, reviewed contribution to a maintainer-confirmed problem demonstrates more than three brilliant architecture proposals. The pragmatic move is:

- Open the checkpoint-scaling discussion with benchmark evidence.
- Meanwhile, claim a bounded maintainer-approved issue—such as the duplicate transcript-compaction work in #2091—and ship it exceptionally well.
- Use that merged contribution to earn trust while the larger idea is discussed.

content.text:
Yes—after checking current `upstream/main`, the strongest unexplored gap is no longer session overlap or handoff metadata.

The best contribution area is:

## Make multi-agent reviews snapshot-consistent

Today, `entire review` can launch multiple reviewers concurrently, but they inspect the live working tree rather than one immutable review snapshot.

The failure looks like this:

```text
t0  Review starts with dirty state A
t1  Reviewer 1 reads state A
t2  User/agent edits the worktree → state B
t3  Reviewer 2 reads state B
t4  Judge combines both reports as if they reviewed the same change
t5  Manifest records the result without enough scope identity to expose the mismatch
```

This is a correctness problem, not an optional convenience.

Evidence from current main:

- [`RunMulti` launches reviewers concurrently](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/review/run_multi.go#L83-L149).
- [The review scope explicitly includes live uncommitted changes](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/review/prompt.go#L28-L79).
- [The local manifest records `StartingSHA` and an absolute worktree path](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/review/manifest.go#L40-L50), but not resolved base SHA, ending tree state, dirty-state fingerprint, or whether the scope drifted.
- Codex, Claude, Gemini and Pi reviewer invocations are not explicitly made read-only. Their behavior may depend on the user’s agent configuration.
- The judge then combines all successful reviewer text into one synthesis prompt as though every report refers to the same code state.

This also aligns cleanly with competitors:

- Cursor gives concurrent tasks isolated worktrees specifically to prevent shared-state conflicts. [Cursor worktrees](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees)
- Cursor warns that subagents sharing one checkout can overwrite or interfere with one another. [Cursor subagents](https://cursor.com/docs/subagents)
- Code.Storage presents isolated disposable Git state, resumable agent state and parallel attempts as core agent infrastructure. [Code.Storage overview](https://code.storage/docs/getting-started/introduction)
- Cursor Origin’s scaling direction is immutable, transactional Git state rather than coordinating agents around one mutable checkout. [Git at any scale](https://cursor.com/blog/git-at-any-scale)

### Proposed issue

**Title:** `Make multi-agent reviews evaluate one immutable review scope`

Core invariant:

> Every reviewer and judge participating in one review run must evaluate the same base, head, and working-tree content.

The issue should describe three distinct risks:

1. User edits during a review produce inconsistent reviewer inputs.
2. A reviewer capable of using tools may modify what later reviewers see.
3. Results cannot currently prove which exact dirty state was reviewed.

### Significant first PR

I would not try to build the entire isolated-worktree system immediately. The first PR can introduce a real correctness boundary:

```go
type ReviewScope struct {
    BaseRef             string
    BaseSHA             string
    HeadSHA             string
    WorktreeFingerprint string
    CapturedAt          time.Time
}
```

The implementation would:

1. Resolve the base ref to a commit SHA before fan-out.
2. Capture `HEAD`.
3. Hash the staged, unstaged and relevant untracked review inputs.
4. Pass one `ReviewScope` through every reviewer and the judge.
5. Recalculate the fingerprint before synthesis and publishing.
6. If it changed, mark the run `drifted` and refuse to present the aggregate as a valid review of one scope.
7. Persist the scope and drift state in the local manifest.
8. Display it in `entire review --findings`.

A deterministic test would use two fake reviewers:

- reviewer A reads immediately;
- reviewer B waits;
- the test changes a file between them;
- Entire must detect drift and must not emit an apparently valid aggregate verdict.

That is a meaningful PR: schema, runtime invariant, user-facing behavior and a reproducible concurrency test. A follow-up can create an immutable synthetic Git tree and isolated reviewer worktrees.

## Other genuinely useful gaps

| Rank | Gap | Value | Recommendation |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | Snapshot-consistent multi-agent reviews | 9/10 | Best issue + first PR |
| 2 | Stable identity for review findings | 8.5/10 | Excellent bounded follow-up |
| 3 | Bound multi-reviewer aggregation | 8/10 | Strong reliability contribution |
| 4 | Scale checkpoint discovery by requested history | 7.5/10 | Benchmark before proposing |
| 5 | Best-of-N candidate comparison | 7/10 | Strong product idea, discuss first |

### 2. Stable review-target identity

Local review history is effectively keyed by an absolute `WorktreePath`.

Consequences:

- Move a Git worktree and its previous findings can disappear from the default listing.
- A `--target` review is stored according to the invoking worktree rather than a durable identity of the reviewed change.
- The manifest cannot clearly answer: “Which branch, base SHA, head SHA and dirty state did this finding review?”

Proposed issue:

**“Persist stable target and scope identity for local review findings”**

Manifest v2 could add:

```text
repository identity
worktree ID
reviewed branch/ref
resolved base SHA
head SHA
dirty-state fingerprint
scope status: current | stale | drifted
```

This is likely the safest first contribution if we decide immutable review execution is too architectural.

### 3. Unbounded review fan-in

The current multi-review path accumulates reviewer events and places successful reviewers’ complete assistant output into the judge prompt. The number of agents and total output can grow substantially.

Possible outcomes:

- memory growth;
- synthesis exceeding context limits;
- failure only after all reviewers have already consumed time and tokens;
- continuously growing local review manifests.

A good issue would be:

**“Bound multi-agent review aggregation without silently dropping findings”**

The solution should include explicit budgets and truncation metadata—not an invisible string slice. Preserve structured findings, record omitted-byte counts and expose whether synthesis used incomplete output.

### 4. Checkpoint discovery scaling

PRs `#1771` and `#1956` improve remote discovery and lazy hydration, but they do not appear to eliminate enumeration of the full checkpoint-ref namespace before branch-history filtering.

This remains legitimate, but we should not lead with a claim until we produce a benchmark:

```text
1,000 checkpoint refs
10,000 checkpoint refs
100,000 checkpoint refs
request last 10 checkpoints from one short branch
```

The invariant should be:

> Work required to request N checkpoints from a branch should primarily follow that branch’s requested history, not the repository’s total checkpoint population.

Cursor Origin and Code.Storage both reinforce that high-concurrency agent storage eventually makes reference and metadata enumeration a fundamental scaling concern.

### 5. Best-of-N implementation comparison

Cursor already exposes the product idea: run multiple candidates in isolated worktrees and compare them. Code.Storage describes parallel attempts from one commit and promoting the best result.

Entire has many of the required primitives:

- checkpoints;
- worktrees and trails;
- agent attribution;
- token and session metadata;
- multi-agent review.

A future command could be:

```bash
entire review --compare candidate-a candidate-b candidate-c
```

It would compare correctness, tests, diff scope, checkpoint provenance and cost, then recommend a candidate without automatically merging it.

This would connect extremely well with LegionCode: LegionCode creates N isolated implementations; Entire preserves and compares their development context. But it is product-direction work, so I would not implement it without maintainer agreement.

## My recommendation

Open the snapshot-consistency issue and a draft PR together. Phrase the PR as a first executable design slice, not as an attempt to bypass maintainers:

> This draft accompanies the design issue and demonstrates the proposed invariant with a deterministic failing reproduction. I’m opening it early so discussion can happen against working code; I’m happy to adjust the contract before marking it ready.

This approach shows exactly what the CTO asked for: you found a concurrency correctness gap, derived an invariant, created a reproduction, chose a bounded first slice, and left the larger architectural choice open for maintainers.

The session-overlap feature should remain dropped. Durable handoff segments should remain a future discussion. Snapshot-consistent review is much more concrete, reproducible, and connected to Entire’s newly expanding multi-agent functionality.

content.text:
You are mostly right. I overstated the danger earlier.

The selector in your screenshot answers:

> “Which set of changes should I display?”

It does not necessarily mean:

> “Freeze these exact file contents for the entire duration of every reviewer.”

## Your example

Start at commit `C0`.

### Turn 1

Codex changes 75 files but commits nothing.

```text
Committed state: C0
Working tree:    W1
Uncommitted diff: C0 → W1, covering 75 files
```

### Turn 2

In the same Codex task, you send another prompt. Codex modifies 10 of those 75 files to fix mistakes.

```text
Working tree: W2
```

The review selector now provides several views:

- **Last Turn:** approximately the changes attributed to the most recent assistant turn, `W1 → W2`.
- **Uncommitted:** the combined current working-tree result, `C0 → W2`.
- **Unstaged:** current changes outside Git’s index.
- **Staged:** changes currently in Git’s index.
- **Committed/Branch:** committed Git history relative to a selected commit or branch.

The official documentation confirms that the review panel reflects repository state—including changes made by Codex, you, or anything else—and that Last Turn selects the assistant’s most recent changes. [OpenAI code-review documentation](https://developers.openai.com/es-419/docs/code-review#qué-cambios-muestra)

Small terminology correction: one Codex **task/chat** contains multiple **turns**. Your second prompt in the same task creates another turn; it is not normally a second task.

## What Entire sees

If you run `entire review` after Turn 2 has finished, Entire instructs reviewers to examine:

```text
commits unique to this branch
+
current uncommitted working-tree changes
```

Therefore all 75 files are in scope, containing their final `W2` contents. The 10 corrected files are not double-counted as separate versions. They simply appear in their latest state.

If nothing changes while the review runs:

```text
Reviewer A → W2
Reviewer B → W2
Reviewer C → W2
Judge      → combines reports about W2
```

That is completely fine. An immutable snapshot provides almost no user-visible benefit here.

## The narrower failure case

The potential problem starts only if the working tree changes while the concurrent review is running:

```text
10:00:00  Entire review starts against W2
10:00:02  Reviewer A reads auth.go from W2
10:00:08  Another task/editor changes auth.go → W3
10:00:12  Reviewer B reads auth.go from W3
10:00:20  Judge combines A and B as one review
```

Reviewer A might say:

> Missing authorization check in `auth.go`.

Reviewer B might say:

> Authorization is correct, but the new fallback is unsafe.

Both could be correct for the bytes they saw, but they did not review the same change.

The review panel selector does not necessarily prevent this. It selects a Git diff scope; it is not proof that external agent processes received one frozen copy of every file.

Also, Codex’s own `/review` is documented as using a dedicated reviewer that reports findings without modifying the working tree. That reduces one source of risk. The remaining concern is another task, editor, formatter, generator, hook, or user changing the checkout during a long Entire review.

## Five arguments supporting the idea

1. **Consensus requires identical evidence**

   If Entire combines three reports into a single verdict, those reports should describe the same source state. Otherwise, “two reviewers approve” is not meaningful.

2. **Uncommitted state has no Git identity**

   A commit has a SHA. Dirty working-tree state does not. Recording only `HEAD` cannot prove which version of uncommitted files was reviewed.

3. **Parallel reviewers increase the timing window**

   One quick reviewer has limited exposure. Multiple reviewers with different models and runtimes may inspect a repository minutes apart.

4. **It improves reproducibility**

   When someone opens findings later, Entire could state:

   ```text
   Base: abc123
   Head: def456
   Working-tree fingerprint: 9da…
   Status: unchanged during review
   ```

   That makes a bug report or disagreement much easier to investigate.

5. **It matters more as review becomes agentic**

   Reviewers may run tests, generators and repository tools. Even when instructed not to edit source, those operations can alter generated files, lockfiles or artifacts. A stable scope becomes more valuable as the workflow grows.

## Five arguments roasting the idea

1. **The failure window is narrow**

   It only matters when something changes during the review. Most developers can simply wait until the review finishes.

2. **It does not solve your 75-files-plus-10-files example**

   Your example works correctly already. Entire should review the final combined working tree, not preserve Turn 1’s broken version.

3. **A complete snapshot is surprisingly complicated**

   It must correctly handle:

   - staged and unstaged versions of the same file;
   - untracked files;
   - deleted and renamed files;
   - submodules;
   - Git LFS;
   - sparse checkouts;
   - ignored generated files.

   That is considerable machinery for an uncommon race.

4. **Read-only isolation may break useful review work**

   Reviewers often need to compile code, run tests or create temporary artifacts. A strictly immutable/read-only checkout can cause otherwise useful reviews to fail.

5. **Simple drift detection may be enough**

   Entire could hash the scope at the beginning and end:

   ```text
   review started: fingerprint A
   review ended:   fingerprint B
   ```

   If they differ, report:

   > Working tree changed during review; findings may refer to different revisions.

   That captures most of the value without manufacturing snapshot commits and worktrees.

## Honest verdict

I would downgrade this from **9/10 to approximately 6.5/10** as a first contribution.

It is a real consistency property, but your objection is correct: normal iterative work before invoking `entire review` is not a problem. Only concurrent mutation during the actual review is problematic.

The sensible first slice would be **review-scope drift detection**, not immutable reviewer worktrees:

1. Fingerprint the selected diff at review start.
2. Run reviewers normally.
3. Fingerprint it again before synthesis.
4. If it changed, visibly mark the review as drifted.
5. Record both fingerprints in the findings manifest.
6. Add a deterministic test that mutates a file between two fake reviewers.

That is useful and proportionate. But I would not yet make it our headline contribution unless we reproduce the race and demonstrate that Entire publishes a genuinely misleading combined result. Otherwise, we should keep digging for a higher-impact gap.

content.text:
Yes—you’re right. We should drop the immutable-review-snapshot idea.

I was mixing two different concerns:

1. **What code exists now?** → Git working-tree diff.
2. **How did the agent arrive there?** → Entire checkpoints/session history.

## Your 75-file example

```text
HEAD
 │
 ├─ Turn 1: agent changes 75 files
 │    └─ Entire records turn/session checkpoint information
 │
 ├─ Turn 2: agent corrects 10 of those files
 │    └─ Entire records newer turn/session information
 │
 └─ Current working tree
      └─ Final uncommitted state of those 75 files
```

`entire review` reviews the **final net state**:

```text
HEAD → current working tree
```

It does not review:

```text
Turn 1 diff
+
Turn 2 diff
```

Therefore it does not double-count the 10 files. It sees their newest contents.

This is the correct behavior for code review: review what would be committed now.

## Where checkpoints fit

Entire checkpoints preserve the development history surrounding that final code:

- prompts;
- agent/session identity;
- transcript;
- summaries;
- files touched;
- token information;
- intermediate session state;
- local shadow-branch snapshots.

At agent turn end, Entire saves an ephemeral/live checkpoint on a worktree-specific shadow branch. When the corresponding work is committed, it condenses that context into a persistent checkpoint associated with the Git commit.

The review command already adds checkpoint information to reviewer prompts in two forms:

- **Committed checkpoints in review scope:** checkpoint IDs, summaries or prompt fallbacks, with instructions to use `entire checkpoint explain <id>` for more detail.
- **Current uncommitted session:** session ID, agent name, touched-file count and latest prompt for qualifying sessions in the current worktree.

See [`review_context.go`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/07785974296adfa7b3d85b5f3b26ea00f27df08a/cmd/entire/cli/review_context.go).

So the division is:

| Question | Source |
|---|---|
| What code should be reviewed? | Current Git diff |
| What changed in the latest Codex turn? | Codex Last Turn view |
| Why was this code changed? | Entire checkpoint/session context |
| What happened during earlier turns? | Entire transcript and checkpoints |
| What would be committed now? | Uncommitted/staged Git state |

One nuance: `entire review` does **not** automatically replay every intermediate file version to every reviewer. It provides bounded checkpoint summaries and identifiers. Reviewers can inspect detailed checkpoint context when needed.

That is sensible. Giving every intermediate version to every reviewer would add noise and consume context.

## Your worktree objection is also correct

If you create multiple Codex tasks and each receives its own worktree:

```text
Task A → worktree A → Entire review A
Task B → worktree B → Entire review B
Task C → worktree C → Entire review C
```

Task B cannot mutate the physical files being inspected in worktree A, even when both modify the same relative path:

```text
worktree-A/apps/web/foo.ts
worktree-B/apps/web/foo.ts
```

Those are separate filesystem objects.

Entire also deliberately namespaces its live shadow branches by worktree. Its architecture documentation says different Git worktrees get different shadow-branch namespaces.

The race I described remains technically possible when:

- two tasks intentionally share one checkout;
- the user edits that checkout while a review is running;
- a formatter or generator changes it;
- tasks are configured to run directly in the same saved project rather than separate worktrees.

But in your worktree-isolated Codex/LegionCode workflow, that is an edge case—not a compelling product gap.

## Final verdict

Reject this contribution idea.

Why:

- It does not solve your normal multi-turn scenario.
- Checkpoints already carry the historical context.
- Git already provides the correct final review state.
- Separate worktrees provide concurrent-task isolation.
- Snapshotting every review would add complexity for a race users can mostly avoid.
- A drift warning would be defensive polish, not the significant contribution we want.

The mistake was treating “live working tree” as inherently unsafe. In Entire’s actual model, it is the correct review target, while checkpoints explain its history and worktrees isolate concurrent implementations.

We should keep looking for a gap where checkpoints, worktrees, trails, and multi-agent review fail in a normal supported workflow—not manufacture protection for an unusual shared-checkout race.

content.text:
I dug through current code, recent issues/PRs, remote branches, and git history. We finally have two defensible gaps—not speculative workflow changes—and one smaller correctness bug.

## Ranked candidates

| Rank | Contribution | Confidence | Scope |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | Make `dispatch --local` work with Entire-native repositories | High | Significant, bounded |
| 2 | Make temporary checkpoints inspectable as immutable code changes | High | Larger, needs UX agreement |
| 3 | Fix legal 26-character names being mistaken for ULIDs | Very high | Small/medium correctness fix |

### 1. Entire-native repositories break `dispatch --local`

This is my recommended first contribution.

Entire now supports its own repository URLs:

```text
entire://cell/et/acme/web
```

But dispatch still assumes every repository is GitHub:

- [`resolveRepoFullName`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/dispatch/mode_local.go:477>) calls the GitHub-only parser.
- It explicitly returns: `dispatch currently supports GitHub origin remotes only`.
- Dispatch also constructs every repository link as `https://github.com/...`.

Meanwhile, Entire already has the correct abstraction in [`gitremote.go`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/gitremote/gitremote.go:24>). It understands:

- ordinary GitHub remotes;
- Entire URLs backed by GitHub, with forge `gh`;
- Entire-native repositories, with forge `et`.

#### Reproduction

```bash
git remote set-url origin entire://cell/et/acme/web
entire dispatch --local
```

Expected: local checkpoints are dispatched.

Actual: dispatch fails before reading them because the origin is not GitHub.

This is particularly credible because it is an internal product inconsistency: Entire added native repositories, but one of its agentic workflows cannot use them.

#### Meaningful first slice

The PR should not merely replace one parser call. It should introduce a proper repository identity:

```go
type repoIdentity struct {
    Forge string
    Owner string
    Repo  string
    URL   string
}
```

Then:

1. Parse origins with the existing `gitremote` package.
2. Group using `forge + owner + repo`, preventing `gh/acme/web` and `et/acme/web` collisions.
3. Produce GitHub links only for GitHub-backed repositories.
4. Preserve a safe native Entire URL—or omit the web link—when no browser URL is known.
5. Add table-driven tests for direct GitHub, Entire GitHub mirrors, Entire-native repos, invalid remotes, and cross-forge name collisions.

#### The roast

The only uncertain detail is how an Entire-native repository should be linked in the rendered output. That is a small maintainer decision, not a reason to reject native dispatch itself. We can isolate URL presentation behind one helper.

This is also the cleanest connection to Cursor Origin: if Entire is becoming a forge and orchestration layer, its own agent workflows cannot remain GitHub-only.

---

### 2. Temporary checkpoints exist, but their code changes are not inspectable

This is a better version of the previous “review snapshot” idea. There is no live-working-tree race here.

Entire already creates an immutable shadow commit for a temporary checkpoint. However, [`explainTemporaryCheckpoint`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:1632>) displays:

- checkpoint identity;
- intent/summary;
- transcript with `--verbose`.

It does not display the files or code captured by that checkpoint. The implementation even calls the no-summary renderer with a `nil` file list.

Also, JSON export in [`explain_export.go`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/explain_export.go:87>) effectively handles committed checkpoints, not temporary checkpoint shadow commits as equal inspection targets.

There is already a test fixture in [`explain_test.go`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/explain_test.go:605>) that:

1. commits `temp.txt`;
2. modifies it;
3. creates a temporary checkpoint;
4. checks only the summary and hint—not the captured file change.

#### Example

An agent makes changes across 75 files and creates checkpoint `C1`. It then fixes 10 of those files and creates `C2`.

The useful immutable views are:

```text
C1 parent tree → C1 shadow tree
C2 parent tree → C2 shadow tree
```

This does not double-count files and does not inspect a moving working tree. Each comparison uses Git objects that already exist.

Possible commands:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain <temporary-checkpoint> --verbose
entire checkpoint explain <temporary-checkpoint> --json
entire checkpoint diff <temporary-checkpoint>
```

#### Why competitors matter

- [Code.Storage live diffs](https://code.storage/docs/guides/live-diffs.md) treats agent state as inspectable diffs.
- [Code.Storage commit diff](https://code.storage/docs/reference/api/commits/get-commit-diff.md) exposes immutable commit comparisons.
- [Cloudflare Artifacts](https://developers.cloudflare.com/artifacts/) makes isolated agent work reviewable and mergeable.
- [Cursor worktrees](https://cursor.com/docs/configuration/worktrees) similarly makes an isolated task reviewable before applying it.

Entire has the immutable object already. The missing part is exposing its code content consistently.

#### Important history

Entire previously had something called `checkpoint diff`, but it compared checkpoint metadata—file-set additions/removals, token changes, checkpoint count. Commit `9ae164e24` removed that work as out of scope for another PR.

Therefore, we must not claim “checkpoint diff has never been considered.” Our proposal is different:

> Inspect the actual immutable code captured in a temporary checkpoint and give temporary checkpoints parity with committed checkpoints.

#### The roast

This has more UX and security questions:

- Should `--verbose` show only file names or a full patch?
- Should patches sanitize terminal control characters?
- Must external Git diff drivers and `textconv` be disabled?
- Should the default comparison be parent-to-checkpoint or session-base-to-checkpoint?

My recommendation is a first slice containing shared target resolution, changed-file output, and JSON parity. Discuss full patch rendering before implementing it.

---

### 3. Legal names can be mistaken for ULIDs

[`looksLikeULID`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/resolveref.go:30>) checks:

- length is 26;
- every character belongs to the Crockford Base32 alphabet.

But that does not fully validate a ULID. Because a ULID contains 128 bits encoded into 130 textual bits, its first character must be `0`–`7`.

A legal project or repository name such as:

```text
REDACTED
```

is 26 allowed characters and begins with `a`. It cannot be a valid ULID, but the CLI classifies it as an ID and skips name lookup.

This affects the shared organization/project/repository reference resolution.

The checkpoint ID package already performs the correct leading-character validation, so there is an internal implementation to reuse or mirror.

This was briefly mentioned as an out-of-scope follow-up in an old merged PR, but it remains unfixed and has no active implementation branch. It is an excellent correctness PR, though probably not substantial enough to be your flagship contribution.

## What I eliminated

I would not spend more time on:

- concurrent-session file-overlap warnings;
- immutable snapshots for `entire review`;
- restoring removed rewind behavior;
- pushing raw shadow snapshots remotely;
- durable local/cloud execution-segment metadata;
- CI webhook commands;
- generic subagent support.

Some are deliberate product decisions; others are already being implemented on open or remote branches. Your criticism of the earlier gaps was correct.

## Recommended move

Start with the native-repository dispatch bug. It has the best combination:

- straightforward reproduction;
- directly connected to Entire’s current forge direction;
- meaningful agentic functionality;
- existing abstractions that demonstrate architectural understanding;
- no active issue, PR, or remote implementation found;

content.text:
You’re right to challenge #1. Both local and cloud dispatch explicitly require a GitHub `origin`, and the output builds GitHub links. That looks like a deliberate current product boundary, even though `--local` reads local checkpoints. I overstated it as a bug. **Skip it unless maintainers say native Entire repos are in scope for dispatch.**

**#2 is not issue [#1139](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/1139).** That issue concerns moving checkpoint storage to a separate remote: checkpoints still push to `origin`, and transcripts become unavailable in the web UI. A maintainer confirmed the owner-mismatch fallback is intentional but called the UI behavior a bug. The issue remains open.

The temporary-checkpoint inspection gap is separate and **not resolved in the code I checked**: [`explainTemporaryCheckpoint`](</Users/puneetpalsingh/Documents/Code/OSSplayground/Entire/cli/cmd/entire/cli/explain.go:1632>) shows the prompt and transcript, but passes no files to its renderer; JSON explain also does not treat the shadow commit as an equivalent checkpoint target. That said, I would **not open an issue yet**. We need to demonstrate a task where inspecting that checkpoint’s code is materially better than `git diff` or the existing review view. Otherwise it risks being another feature nobody needs.

**#3: skip as the flagship contribution.** The ULID-name misclassification is real, but the code explicitly acknowledges the trade-off, and it is a relatively small edge-case fix. Keep it as a possible quick follow-up PR, not the contribution meant to show the CTO how you think.

So: **none of these three is ready to be our big issue + PR.** Your objections improved the filter. We should keep hunting for a reproduced, consequential failure rather than force a contribution out of this list.
So you are saying, This repos is so perfect that we cant even find one bug, or new functionality to add to this repo?

No. I’m saying I gave you weak candidates and then defended them too confidently. A fast-moving CLI with hooks, checkpoint storage, worktrees, and new forge features will have gaps; I haven’t earned a claim about which one is worth your PR yet. I’m going back to a concrete failure path and will separate reproducible bugs from product choices.

No, bro. The repo is not perfect. I was applying the wrong filter: I kept rejecting real bugs because someone had *noticed* them, when the useful question is whether anyone has **fixed and owned** them.

Here is one concrete example on current upstream `main`: Entire’s [multi-push-URL integration tests](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/main/cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/multi_pushurl_test.go) still contain two `KNOWN BUG` skips. In one, adding a fresh mirror can push Entire’s metadata branch **before the user’s code branch**, causing the forge to select the metadata branch as its default. In the other, independently diverged mirrors do not both recover; one silently stops receiving checkpoints. These are reproduced failure cases, not feature pitches.

The honest caveat: a maintainer already documented them in [PR #1897](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1897). They are **not our discoveries**. But an unfixed, consequential bug with a ready-made regression test could still make an excellent contribution: remove the skip, implement the fix, and show why checkpoint data and the user’s push remain safe.

So I retract the implication that we must invent an unseen feature to contribute meaningfully. We can pursue a substantial fix that is known but unowned, while continuing to look for a genuinely new gap. I should have brought you this evidence earlier instead of repeatedly selling speculative ideas.
